Meriem Boundaoui, 15 ans, a été tuée le: Meriem Boundaoui, 15, was killed on February 7, 2021.
<strong>Un an. C’est le temps qui s’est: One year. That is how much time has passed since Meriem Boundaoui lost her life in a bakery parking lot in Saint-Léonard. On February 7, 2021, the 15-year-old was shot dead while sitting in her friend’s vehicle. The hope of seeing this crime solved? Her sister, Safia Boundaoui, is starting to lose it. “[The investigators] come to the house sometimes, but until when?” she wonders. For the loved ones of victims like Safia, hope is hard to sustain. How can they manage it? Is the homicide clearance rate lower in Montréal than elsewhere? La Converse investigated.
Meriem était la plus jeune des sœurs Bou: Meriem was the youngest of the Boundaoui sisters. She came to Canada hoping to find a better future. She dreamed of becoming a teacher and buying a store for her father, who stayed behind in Algeria. For the young girl, Canada was a land of dreams. “She cried to come to Canada,” Safia tells us at her home. A sign made last year during a commemoration day sits in Safia’s living room. “I was only 15…” it reads. It bears the face of the young girl, which travelled across the country. A year later, the Boundaoui family lives with the same pain. “I can’t stop mourning her. Sometimes, when I don’t feel like doing something, I think of her and I do it for her. Just for her, because she left us too young,” Safia tells us as she looks at the sign, while a little blue bird named Meriem sings at the entrance of the house. It was bought after the young girl’s death.
Pour pouvoir calmer sa douleur, la famil: To ease their pain, the family of the deceased is asking for the crime to be solved. But after a year, they struggle to understand why it still isn’t. The investigation is ongoing, and no charges have been laid. Safia is in regular contact with Montréal police investigators. She says she trusts the police, but that trust is starting to erode. In her view, the investigators haven’t done enough. “As long as the case stays buried, it’s hard. They come to the house, but until when?” she asks. “It’s been a year since my sister died and there’s been no arrest… Yet the place where she was was really suspicious. We hear about it. After a year, why haven’t they found anything?”
Plusieurs personnes du quartier ainsi qu: Several people in the neighbourhood, as well as the police, have heard about certain suspects. Names have been named. “There are rumours going around. In the neighbourhood, these thugs are known, people know them, the police know them too,” says a source close to the deceased. The shooting was reportedly retaliation for a conflict between two groups of youth that took place a few days before Meriem’s murder.
La Converse a communiqué avec le princip: La Converse contacted the lead investigator on the young girl’s murder, Detective Sergeant François Baillargeon, to try to understand where the investigation stood. He told us by phone that he could not comment so as not to jeopardize his investigation. “I know everything that’s being said on the street, and probably more than you do,” he nevertheless let us know. On the slow pace of the investigation, he explained that “in some countries, the burden of proof is lower, but in Canada, the burden of proof is very high; we don’t want to put innocent people in prison.”
<strong>Taux de résolution des homicides: Lower homicide clearance rate in Montréal in 2021
En 2021, Montréal a connu une augmentati: In 2021, Montréal saw a sharp increase in gun violence. In all, 35 homicides were recorded, the highest number since 2010. Yet even though the metropolis has more police officers per capita than any other major city in the country, barely half of the cases considered homicides led to charges in 2021. According to national data gathered by La Converse, this proportion is well below the percentage of homicide cases resulting in charges in almost every major Canadian city. While fewer than half of murders in Montréal led to charges in 2021, nearly three-quarters did in Toronto.
Paul Laurier, qui a navigué dans le syst: Paul Laurier, who navigated the Quebec justice system for years as an investigator, knows its strengths and weaknesses. In Quebec, “the police build the evidence, put the files on the prosecutor’s desk, and it’s the prosecutor who authorizes the charges,” he explains. What Mr. Laurier calls the “prosecutor’s desk” is the Director of Criminal and Penal Prosecutions (DPCP). The DPCP acts as a bridge between the police and the justice system. Case files and evidence are submitted to it so that it can determine whether charges should be laid against the suspect or suspects. “The DPCP adds a layer. That’s not necessarily bad,” says the former investigator, qualifying his point.
Mais si on regarde ce qui se fait à Toro: But if we look at what is done in Toronto, where proportionally more murders led to charges in 2021, we may wonder whether the Ontario justice system, which has no equivalent of the DPCP, makes it easier to lay criminal charges. “In Ontario, it’s the police who directly charge [criminals]. The prosecutors are there to coach them,” Mr. Laurier explains. “The state follows and backs [the police] on that.” The former investigator believes this approach can more easily lead to trials of accused people. He cites as an example Jian Ghomeshi’s 2016 sexual assault trial, which, despite the charges against him, did not end in a conviction. “In Quebec, that trial would probably never have taken place,” he says. In short, even if police can themselves bring people before the courts, that doesn’t necessarily translate into more guilty verdicts. Mr. Laurier nonetheless considers the Quebec justice system “sick.” “The delays are unbelievable, and the police are at a disadvantage [during the judicial process],” he says. He cites certain technical details that force police services to “close” their evidence within prescribed deadlines. “Back in the day, we could make arrests, and the follow-up investigation came afterward. Now, we can’t do that anymore. […] In terms of the rights of the crook versus the rights of the family, it’s the rights of the accused that win out. […] Meanwhile, the crooks have the upper hand,” he observes.
Un constat que font aussi avec amertume: Meriem Boundaoui’s loved ones share this bitter assessment. What worries them is that they are not the only ones mourning young people who fall to bullets. “After Meriem’s murder, how many others were shot dead? It’s the same thing,” Safia laments. She believes that if her sister’s murder isn’t solved, gun violence becomes normalized. “These young people who shoot, they’re immune to advice; even if you give it to them, they won’t listen. In their heads, they see death, they see weapons, it’s their way of life. […] So if they kill once, it becomes very easy for them. They get past the threshold of fear, they become bold. It’s as if we’re normalizing it,” she says with emotion. Safia doesn’t wish harm on the person who shot her sister, but she is asking for justice so that others don’t follow his example. “Don’t you believe the crime will be solved?” we ask her. “After 10, 15 years maybe, when everyone has forgotten everything,” she confides. “I met a woman; her son was killed two years ago in Montréal, and she comforted us,” she continues. “She has been mourning her son for two years, and she has no news about the culprit. That’s why I tell myself that, 15 years from now, we may perhaps have news about who killed Meriem… Sometimes I wonder why, in a developed country, they are so incapable of solving a crime…” Safia wonders.
Plusieurs experts s’accordent pour dire: Several experts agree that trust in a police force plays a major role in solving crimes committed on its territory. “Obviously, we can say that if there is a lot of trust in the police, people will go to the police more, they will cooperate with them more and they will participate more overall in public safety,” says Massimiliano Mulone, associate professor at the School of Criminology at the Université de Montréal. The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) has seen that trust erode over the past few years. According to a 2020 survey by the firm Angus Reid, only 67% of Montréal residents view the SPVM favourably. That is the worst rate among Canada’s 10 largest cities.
Pour l’enquêteur à la retraite Paul Laur: For retired investigator Paul Laurier, the 2021 crime clearance statistics are more of a “statistical anomaly” than a consequence of the public’s declining trust in the SPVM. Almost 90% of the murders committed in Montréal the previous year, in 2020, had been solved. “It’s hard to investigate [these days],” says the man who worked for the Sûreté du Québec for more than 20 years. “Just because there are no charges doesn’t mean the case isn’t being investigated or that the sources aren’t considered credible,” he points out.
Le type de meurtre pourrait expliquer la: The type of murder could explain the low clearance rate in 2021, according to criminologist Massimiliano Mulone. “I’m not sure we can draw such a direct correlation [between public trust and solving murders]. For 2021, it’s possible that some of the homicides [in Montréal] were linked to internal wars within organized crime. Those homicides are much harder to solve,” the researcher explains. Paul Laurier also raises this hypothesis. He attributes the low clearance rate to the recent wave of violence tied to the proliferation of firearms. “2021 was catastrophic,” he concludes.
Au Collège de Maisonneuve, on rencontre: At Collège de Maisonneuve, we meet Mohamed Mimoun, who works as a student support worker and coordinates the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel. He knows well the issues young people in these neighbourhoods face. Many confide in him. He explains this lack of trust to us. Mr. Mimoun is not surprised by the low clearance rate for gun violence–related crimes in Montréal. “I get the impression that the police aren’t able to get information, and that if they do, they can’t get a clear statement from someone who can provide evidence […] The youth are closed off. If they witness something, they’d rather go take revenge themselves than go to someone to share the information,” he says. He gives the example of young people in Saint-Léonard who were the targets of armed attacks last week and who told him they refuse to talk to the police because they don’t trust them. Same finding after the death of Amir Benayad, the 17-year-old shot on the Plateau-Mont-Royal during a brawl between two groups of youth in January, Mr. Mimoun reports. The young people present know who fired, but don’t want to talk to the police. “There were youth who wanted to avenge their friend instead of going to the police. Why? Because they don’t trust the system,” says the youth worker. “Is it because solving crimes takes too long?” we ask him.
« Je pense qu’ils savent que la police n: “I think they know the police don’t have the power to solve cases, because they’re not connected to the communities; they can’t get into that circle. We’re among communities, we know who did it, but it seems like the police can’t reach that circle to find out who did what. That’s how the youth are starting to see it, like it’s a form of power. They don’t feel protected by the police.” As a result, those who shoot even feel they have more power than the authorities. For Mohamed, this is a consequence of the police’s long-standing neglect of racialized communities. “It’s the consequence of what we haven’t done for years: we’re not connected to the communities. It’s like revenge for the youth, who say to themselves: ‘You’re only here to bother us with arbitrary arrests and profiling. Well, now figure out how to find your criminals, the real ones, not the guy who ran a red light or who hangs out in a park!’”
Malgré le nombre élevé des meurtres non: Despite the high number of unsolved murders, it is hard for the general public to get information on these crimes, because the SPVM limits access to these files. <l1>On its website, only the details of six homicides are available to the public, the most recent dating from 2012.</l1> A quick web search shows that some police services make great use of the internet to solve crimes in their jurisdictions. The Toronto police, for instance, make all this information public. On its website, you can consult both ongoing investigations into murders committed in recent years and “cold” cases, that is, those not under active investigation.
Pour Paul Laurier, diffuser de telles in: For Paul Laurier, publishing this kind of information on the web is a technique worth promoting. “The Toronto police are very active [online]. These are good practices. They’re simple things that don’t cost millions,” he says. Why doesn’t the SPVM make this type of information easier to access? Consulted by email on the subject, the SPVM’s media relations section replied that “this approach has not borne fruit” and that “efforts and resources have since been directed elsewhere to advance investigations.” It also stated that “the SPVM remains constantly on the lookout for the various possible investigative avenues in order to solve unsolved murders.”
<strong>Comment résoudre plus de crimes: How can more crimes be solved and gun violence prevented?
Même s’il est difficile de mettre le doi: Even if it is hard to pinpoint the exact causes of this low clearance rate, the reality for victims’ families doesn’t change. How can these crimes be better solved and peace brought to grieving families? “I think everyone’s goal is the same: to reduce violence and youth delinquency in eastern Montréal. But it comes through building closer ties, it comes through communication,” says Robenson Raphäel, youth worker with the organization Horizon Carrière in Saint-Léonard. We meet him in his office on rue Jean-Talon. Robenson works in the Départ à neuf program, which aims to help young people who have dropped out of school return to their studies or enter the job market. The office is steps from where Meriem Boundaoui was killed a year earlier, right next to the Castel bakery. Since the tragedy, Robenson has noticed a stronger police presence around the building: cadets, mounted police, cameras and patrol officers are often visible. But he believes they need to go further: “For me, going further means going to talk to people, asking them how they feel,” he argues. “The police also have to learn to talk to people in the neighbourhood and to the youth.
Une relation, ce n’est pas une fois par: A relationship isn’t once a year; the approach changes everything.” Robenson thinks we need to work with young people who fall into crime and lose hope in the justice system. “A young person dying is hard. I don’t think a young person wakes up and says to himself: ‘I want to be a criminal.’ The police do their thing, but we also have a role to play with the population,” he says. “We can help young people speak up about things, but it comes through education. Me, I say: ‘If they don’t cooperate with the police, let them cooperate with someone. Because as a young person, there are burdens you carry – it’s very heavy. Sometimes you can’t talk to mom and dad. But there’s still a youth worker, a friend you can talk to. My goal is to tell them we’re here for them, we’re listening and we want to be part of the solution. We’re ready to help them if they want to be helped,” explains the Saint-Léonard youth worker.
Robenson Raphaël convient toutefois que: Robenson Raphaël does agree, however, that youth programs are not always suited to this segment of the population. “Of course, the program was put together years ago, it’s not designed like: ‘If you have guns at home and you shot someone, yo G, get out of the hood and come to us.’ I’ve got some in my program who were in it with both feet, they know what goes on in the street. We want young people to know they can find work and that there are other things they can do to change the course of their lives,” he reminds us.
De retour chez Safia Boundaoui, on lui d: Back at Safia Boundaoui’s home, we ask her what she would like to say to young people who use guns and to the person who killed her sister. “How do you have the courage to pick up a gun? Can you imagine… if someone kills you, do you think about your family, about your parents? Do you have feelings? If you have no feelings, I can’t talk to you. Sometimes we have feelings, but we do it against our will. Do you have feelings in your heart? Tell me, do you still have feelings?” she asks in a trembling voice. She pauses for a moment. “The person who killed my sister, I’d really like to see him. Does he have a conscience? He went and killed someone else. I think that day will never come, I’ll never see this person. If I were in his place, I would turn myself in to the police.” She doesn’t wish him harm, only punishment. “To be able to kill, he’s sick, he’s not right in the head. He’s a victim, I even think of his parents,” she adds.
Meriem Boundaoui enfant, dans son villag: Meriem Boundaoui as a child, in her home village in Algeria.
Safia veut aussi s’adresser aux parents: Safia also wants to address the parents of teenagers and ask them to pay attention to their children’s mental health. “I want to send a message to parents, I want to ask them to keep track of their children, of their mental health. If my son is dangerous, I can detect it, I can know. I’m the first to know my son is dangerous. I can do something for him, to get him help,” observes the mother.
